concept.name: Sample variance
concept.definition: The average squared deviation of sample observations from the sample mean, computed with divisor n - 1 (Bessel's correction). The n - 1 divisor makes it an unbiased estimator of the population variance; the naive n-divisor version is biased downward.
concept.intuition: It is the variance you compute from the data you have, adjusted slightly upward because estimating the mean from the same data eats one degree of freedom.
concept.mechanics: Compute the sample mean, sum the squared deviations from it, and divide by n - 1. Dividing by n instead systematically underestimates sigma^2 by the factor (n-1)/n because the sample mean sits closer to the sample points than the true mean does; its square root is the sample standard deviation.
concept.formula: s^2 = SUM_{i=1..n} (x_i - x_bar)^2 / (n - 1), where x_bar is the sample mean and n the sample size; the uncorrected version (divisor n) has E[S^2] = ((n-1)/n) * sigma^2.
concept.failure_modes: Like all moment-based spread measures it is dominated by tail observations and unreliable for heavy-tailed data; for returns with volatility clustering it also varies strongly across sub-periods, so a single full-sample s^2 averages over regimes. It is undefined (as a population quantity) when the second moment does not exist.
concept.misconceptions: The n - 1 divisor is not a small-sample 'fudge factor' to ignore; it is exactly the correction that removes the downward bias, and with n = 30 the naive estimator is still about 3% low. Also, unbiasedness of s^2 does not carry over to its square root: the sample standard deviation remains slightly biased for sigma.
concept.example: Five daily returns with sum of squared deviations from their mean equal to 0.001 give s^2 = 0.001/4 = 0.00025 (s = 1.58% daily); dividing by n = 5 instead would give 0.0002, an underestimate.
